name: Freya Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine by me. I've got about an hour before I have to pick up a reel of cable from the wholesaler, so let's go.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm lead electrician at Corran Electrical, a four-person firm in Ashby Vale. Most of what we do is rewiring old terraced houses, the ones with rubber cable and fuse boxes older than my gran. I'm in the van by half seven, I lift floorboards, chase walls, run new circuits and test everything before I sign it off. I run the two lads on site and Dev, the owner, does the quotes and the phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a house that was a fire risk is safe, and the family has no idea how close it was. What wears me out is the money. I'm on less than electricians in the city get, the rent on my flat on Mill Street went up again in spring, and I've got maybe three weeks of bills in the bank. My partner Jonah does night shifts at a care home, so we pass each other in the hallway most days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: it's mostly marketing. Someone in a suit sold a lot of software and the rest of us carried on wiring houses. I'd probably post something sarcastic in the union branch group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes for me, and that's not good news either. Nothing changing means I'm still on low pay with three weeks of savings in a town with about three firms. The thing that frightens me in that world is a quiet month, not a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, and I'd push Dev for a proper pay rise in January, because I'm the one signing off the jobs. I'd keep going to the branch meetings, because the union rate is the only thing that's ever moved my pay. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, which I've said every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, mostly. Relief that nobody's coming for the trade, but the same tired feeling about rent and bills. It's not a happy picture, it's just the normal one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a quiet month frightens you. What happens in a quiet month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev cuts the hours, and I'm on hourly. Last February we had two weeks of nothing but call-outs for tripped switches, and I lost about a quarter of my pay. Jonah covered the rent and I hated it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does any of the routine AI stuff touch your day at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's started using some program to write his quotes, he says it saves him an evening a week. I don't touch it. I don't need a computer to tell me how much cable goes into a three-bed house, I can tell you from the doorstep.

say: The AI talk was **mostly marketing**, and electricians carried on wiring houses as before.
Nothing changed for the trade, so the **union rate** still matters more than any software.
think: Nothing changing still leaves me on **low pay** with three weeks of savings.
A **quiet month** frightens me more than any robot, because I'm paid by the hour.
do: Push Dev for a **pay rise** in January, since she signs off every job.
Keep going to the **union branch** meetings every month.
Try again to put **fifty a month** aside for a cushion.
feel: **Flat** and tired rather than scared, with some relief that the trade is left alone.
S0.quote: Nothing changing means I'm still on low pay with three weeks of savings in a town with about three firms.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **money and hours**, not technology; a quiet February already cost her a quarter of her pay.
She **refuses** to touch Dev's quoting program and is proud she can price a job from the doorstep.
The **union** is the only thing she credits with ever raising her pay.

steps.text: Ask Dev for a pay rise in January
Attend the monthly union branch meeting
Set up a fifty-a-month standing order to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who lost out were the office workers, and that somebody should have protected them. You can't rewire a house from a laptop. I'd be at the branch meeting arguing that the union should take in the office staff at the wholesalers, because they're the ones getting hit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm all right for a good while, and I feel a bit guilty saying it. The part that changes is Dev's side: quotes, ordering, booking jobs. If he gets that all done by software, he might decide the firm can take on more work with fewer of us, or he might take on a cheaper lad and give him the app to check his work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the work, and I'd make sure I'm the one who does the testing and certificates, because that's my licence on the line. I'd join the push for a union agreement at Corran, even if it's just four of us. And I'd stop buying lunch from the bakery and take sandwiches, because I don't trust the next few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for my hands, for the people around me. And a bit angry, because nobody asked the people this happens to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a cheaper lad with an app. Is that a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a small one. Our apprentice Callum is good, but if some phone app tells him what he's doing is fine, Dev might think he doesn't need me watching. An app can't smell burnt insulation behind a wall. I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, if not yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonah, actually. They've already brought in a tablet system at the care home that writes the night notes. If they decide one carer and a tablet can cover a floor, he's the one on nights with no say.

say: **Office workers** lost out, and somebody should have protected them before it happened.
The union should **take in office staff** at the wholesalers, because they're the ones being hit.
think: Her own hands-on work is **safe for years**, and she feels a bit guilty about that.
Dev might use software to **run with fewer people** or let a cheaper lad work unchecked.
do: Keep **testing and certificates** firmly in her own hands, because her licence is on the line.
Push for a **union agreement** at Corran, even with only four staff.
Take **packed lunches** instead of buying from the bakery.
feel: **Uneasy** for the people around her more than for herself.
**Angry** that nobody asked the workers this happens to.
S1.quote: An app can't smell burnt insulation behind a wall. I can.
fieldNote: She places the change on **Dev's side** of the firm: quotes, ordering and bookings.
Her real worry shifts to her partner **Jonah**, whose care home already uses a tablet for night notes.
She sees **certification** as her protection, because only a licensed person can sign.

steps.text: Keep doing all testing and certificate sign-offs herself
Push for a written union agreement at Corran Electrical
Take packed lunches instead of buying at the bakery

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly what we warned about, and the government let tech companies run it. I'd be at every protest going. I'd say robots doing wiring by 2031 means the people who own the robots own the trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm done by the time I'm thirty-two, unless something big happens. The first two years, the quotes and planning go, so Dev doesn't need much of an office. Then the robots come for the houses, and I've got no savings and no other skill. I've never even used one of these AI programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the union, because one person on her own has nothing. I'd write to our MP every month asking for a law that says a licensed person signs off every job, robot or not. I'd cut everything I can, the gym, the phone contract, and move in with Jonah's mum if we had to. I wouldn't go and learn the AI stuff, I just wouldn't know where to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, really. The kind where you lie awake doing the maths. And angry. Two years is nothing. You can't even finish a course in two years, and I've never used one of these AI programs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robots come about three years after the thinking AI. What do those three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They mean I'm still working, but watching it come. I'd be wiring houses knowing the clock is running. Maybe I'd take every bit of overtime and put it away, because those three years are my only savings window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car I don't have, ha. No, the gym, then the phone contract, then we'd stop going to see my sister in the city because the train's forty quid. Jonah's mum has a spare room in Kelby, and I'd hate it, but we'd go.

say: This is what the **union warned** about, and the government let tech companies run it.
Whoever owns the **robots** will own the trade by 2031.
think: She expects to be **out of work** by 32, with no savings and no other skill.
Two years isn't even long enough to **finish a course**, so she sees no exit.
do: Throw herself into the **union** and every protest it organises.
Write to the **MP monthly** asking for a law that a licensed person signs every job.
Cut the **gym and phone contract**, and move to Jonah's mum's spare room if needed.
feel: **Angry** that two years leaves no time to prepare.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing. You can't even finish a course in two years, and I've never used one of these AI programs.
fieldNote: The three-year **robot gap** is the only window she sees, and she'd use it for overtime savings.
She turns to **group action and law** rather than learning new tools, which she says she wouldn't know how to start.
She'd accept a move to her **partner's mother's** home, though she'd hate it.

steps.text: Join every union protest and branch campaign
Write to the MP monthly about licensed sign-off law
Cancel the gym and switch to a cheaper phone plan
Move into Jonah's mum's spare room in Kelby

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so let's use them to fight for rules now. Rules on who can sign off electrical work, rules on who pays when a robot burns a house down. I'd say that loudly, at the branch and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps but not much. I'd be thirty-five when the robots arrive, and still on low pay. The thinking part comes first, so Dev's office changes by 2031, and then I've got three more years on the tools. That's eight years of work, and I'd want something at the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every overtime shift and try to get two months of savings by 2030. I'd push the union to get licensed sign-off written into the rules before 2031, while people still listen. And maybe, maybe, I'd do the inspection course, the one for checking other people's work, because that's the thing that still needs a person with a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frozen. Five years is enough to be angry and organised instead of just angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe the inspection course. Why the maybe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I hate classrooms and I hate change, I'll be honest. But inspection is still my trade, just with a clipboard. It's a hundred and eighty quid and four weekends, and I'd have to find both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Callum, the apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to finish his papers and get his licence quick, because a licence is the thing they'll have to respect. I'd tell him not to bet his whole life on the tools like I did.

say: Five years is time to **fight for rules** on who signs off electrical work.
Someone has to answer for **who pays** when a robot burns a house down.
think: Five years helps a bit, but she'd still be on **low pay at 35**.
She counts **eight years** of work left and wants something to show at the end.
do: Take every **overtime** shift to reach two months of savings by 2030.
Push the union for **licensed sign-off** rules before 2031.
Maybe take the **inspection course**: £180 and four weekends.
feel: **Worried** but not frozen; five years lets her be organised, not just angry.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to be angry and organised instead of just angry.
fieldNote: She separates the **thinking AI date** from the robot date and counts eight working years.
The **inspection course** is the only change she'd consider, because it keeps her inside her trade.
Her advice to the **apprentice** reveals regret about betting everything on the tools.

steps.text: Take every overtime shift until 2030 to save two months
Push the union branch for licensed sign-off rules
Book the four-weekend electrical inspection course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for the government to do it properly, so no excuses. Retraining money, a proper wage floor, rules on the robots. If they waste ten years, that's on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is the dangerous one for me. Ten years is long enough that I'd tell myself there's time, and I know myself, I'd keep putting it off. By 2039 I'd be forty, still renting, and the robots would be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the inspection course in the first two years, no excuses. I'd keep going with the union, and I'd vote for whoever promises a proper plan for trades. And I'd want Jonah and me out of renting, so I'd start looking at the council's shared ownership scheme, even though we'd need a deposit we don't have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer than the fast ones, but there's a nag in it. Ten years feels like a lot, and that's what worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep putting it off. What would make you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the union branch ran it as a group, I'd go. I'd go with the others where I wouldn't go on my own. That's just how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does forty look like to you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Best case, I'm an inspector, I've got a small flat with Jonah, and I'm checking robot work for a living. Worst case, I'm forty and renting off the same landlord, with a trade nobody pays for.

say: Ten years means the government has **no excuses** for failing trades.
They need **retraining money**, a proper wage floor and rules on robots.
think: Ten years is dangerous because she'd **keep putting it off**.
By 2039 she'd be **forty and renting**, with robots ready for her trade.
do: Do the **inspection course** within the first two years.
Vote for whoever has a real **plan for trades**.
Look into the council's **shared ownership** scheme with Jonah.
feel: **Calmer** than the fast pictures, with a nag that ten years feels too comfortable.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd tell myself there's time, and I know myself, I'd keep putting it off.
fieldNote: She sees her own **delay** as the main risk in the slow picture.
She'd change only **alongside others**, through a union-run course.
Her best case is to become an **inspector** checking robot work, owning a small flat with Jonah.

steps.text: Finish the electrical inspection course by 2028
Vote for the party with a real plan for trades
Apply to the council's shared ownership scheme with Jonah

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Two years and then robots three years later, and I've got three weeks of savings. What would help is a law that says a licensed electrician signs off every job, and money to retrain that doesn't come out of my wages.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about pay. Everyone talks about robots taking jobs, but for people like me the problem started way before AI. If I was paid properly I'd have savings, and then none of this would scare me as much.

headlineQuote: For people like me the problem started way before AI. If I was paid properly I'd have savings, and then none of this would scare me as much.
portrait: Freya is a 27-year-old **lead electrician** rewiring old terraced houses for a four-person firm in Ashby Vale.
She's on **low hourly pay** with three weeks of savings, renting on Mill Street with her partner Jonah.
She never uses AI and **leans on the union** and the law rather than new tools.
She shifts from **uneasy** in the mild pictures to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
In slower pictures she'd reluctantly train as an **inspector**, but fears she'd keep putting it off.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach her trade around 2031 while she has almost no savings.
whatWouldHelp: A law that a **licensed electrician** signs off every job, robot or not.
Retraining money that **doesn't come from wages**, and better pay so she can save.
